finding.claim: Authorization bypass on DELETE /files/<fid>: the guard's return value is ignored. `require_allowed` is an alias of the boolean `is_allowed`, not the aborting `ensure_allowed`, so the check never blocks the delete.
finding.source: Any caller (including unauthenticated, with no or arbitrary X-Session-User-Verified header) sends DELETE /files/<fid> with a known file id.

trace.note: `from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed` aliases the boolean predicate under a name that implies enforcement
is_allowed only returns True/False and never aborts
the result of require_allowed(...) is discarded, with no if/abort

finding.guards_checked: Compared with rename_file, which correctly uses ensure_allowed (aborts with 403). before_request only sets g.user and does not reject anyone. There is no other auth middleware or decorator.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: before_request load_user (views.py:11-12) only sets g.user; require_allowed is is_allowed (a bool predicate, acl.py:4-5) whose result is discarded; ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts but is only used in rename_file
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the boolean is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) as require_allowed, views.py:18 discards its result, and views.py:19 deletes unconditionally, so any caller who can send the request can delete a file whose id they know (a nonexistent id raises KeyError at views.py:17, which only means the id must be valid).

finding.claim: The user identity is taken from a client-supplied HTTP header, X-Session-User-Verified, with no signature, session or token validation. An attacker can impersonate any user who holds grants, including on the rename endpoint, which is otherwise correctly guarded.
finding.source: The X-Session-User-Verified request header, set by the attacker. The precondition is that no upstream proxy strips or overwrites the header; that is not visible in this code.
finding.sink: `ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write")` at views.py:26 and the rename write at views.py:27. The delete at views.py:19 is also affected, though it is already unguarded (F1).

trace.note: g.user is set directly from the header value
g.user is used as the principal in the grants lookup
grants.get(user) trusts the supplied string as the identity
the file is renamed when the spoofed user has the write grant

finding.guards_checked: No signature or session verification was found in the repo. The header name suggests a trusted proxy sets it, but nothing in the code enforces that, and the app does not reject requests that lack it.

verdict.guard_found: Only ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, aborts 403) at views.py:26, which checks grants for the attacker-supplied identity. The delete path uses is_allowed aliased as require_allowed (views.py:4, 18) whose boolean result is discarded, so that path is unguarded (F1). No authentication or signature check exists on the header.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the client header, and acl.py:5 and views.py:26 trust it as the principal, so an anonymous attacker can send the header of any grant-holder and pass ensure_allowed to reach the rename at views.py:27, unless an upstream proxy (not visible in the repo) strips the header.
